idiom_name: Akka Streams MergeSequence (and MergeSorted for pre-sorted sources)
implementation_notes: Akka Streams ships the operator this pattern describes: MergeSequence takes several streams whose elements in aggregate carry a linear sequence number (difference 1, starting at 0) and emits a single stream in that order, which is the resequencer's release rule as a first-class stage; MergeSorted merges two already-sorted streams. Equally important is the order-by-construction default: mapAsync keeps the input order while running the stage in parallel, so a pipeline that must be ordered should not become unordered in the first place. A hand-written stage - Source.queue feeding a SortedMap window with a gap deadline - remains the fallback when the sequence numbers are sparse rather than dense and linear.
code_sketch:
// order by construction: mapAsync keeps input order while running in parallel
Source(msgs).mapAsync(parallelism = 8)(enrich).runWith(Sink.foreach(writeInOrder))

// genuinely scrambled sources: MergeSequence releases a linear sequence in order
Source(partitions)                       // each carries Msg(seq)
  .mergeSubstreams
  .via(MergeSequence[Msg, Long](breadth = 4, _.seq))
  .runWith(Sink.foreach(applyInOrder))
pitfalls: MergeSequence expects a dense linear sequence starting at 0 with difference 1, so sparse or reset sequence numbers stall it; sparse numbering needs a hand-written window instead.
mapAsyncUnordered performs better but destroys the order guarantee that mapAsync gives for free - choosing it silently makes a resequencer necessary again.
A backpressured ordered stage mirrors its slowest element: if one sequence number is delayed, upstream demand stalls for the whole stream and the window is not the only buffer growing.
